title: The third paragraph (Numbers 15:37–41)
hookLine: the fringes, and the Exodus remembered morning and night

cards: People tie strings around fingers. They write on the backs of their hands, set a photo as the lock screen, keep a beach stone in a pocket. Humans are forgetful, and know it, so they hang reminders on their bodies.

The third paragraph of the Shema is about exactly that: a reminder you wear. And in many synagogues, while it's read, people lift the fringes they gathered earlier and kiss them, again and again, at one particular word.

teach.b: The paragraph comes from the Book of Numbers. God tells Moses to have the people make tzitzit, fringes, on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue in each. The reason is given right there.
In the old Jewish translation: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them." Look, remember, do.

teach.h: NOT AFTER YOUR HEART AND EYES.
teach.b: Then a warning: not to go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The eyes see things and the heart wants them; the fringes are a counterweight you can see.
The word tzitzit appears three times in the paragraph, and many people kiss the fringes at each one.
The blue thread, tekhelet, came from a dye whose source was lost for many centuries; some people today wear blue threads again from a dye they believe is the ancient one, while others wear all white.
The paragraph ends with the Exodus: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. That's why it's said at night too, even though fringes are a daytime commandment.

The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, records an old argument: must the Exodus be remembered at night? Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says he couldn't win the point until Ben Zoma read a verse: all the days of your life.
The days of your life means the days.

teach.h: ALL THE DAYS INCLUDES THE NIGHTS.
teach.b: All the days includes the nights.
So the Exodus is remembered twice a day, morning and evening.

how: The third paragraph of the Shema, Numbers 15:37–41, is said morning and evening; in the morning, many people holding their tzitzit kiss them each time the word is said and look at them while reading.

o: yes, because it remembers the Exodus.

practice: Find an object near you that carries a memory, a ring, a photo, a book someone gave you, a child's drawing, and hold it.
Let it remind you who gave it and what it asks of you; then, if it feels right, kiss it or press it to your heart, the way people kiss the fringes. Look, remember, do.
